ai.subject: Microbiology & immunology
ai.summary: Hepatitis C virus (HCV) is an enveloped, single‑stranded RNA virus that infects hepatocytes. It causes a mostly non‑cytopathic, chronic liver disease that progresses from inflammation to fibrosis, cirrhosis, and hepatocellular carcinoma.

sections.p: HCV belongs to the Flaviviridae family (genus Hepacivirus). It replicates in the cytoplasm of liver cells and evades immunity by blocking interferon signalling.
b: RNA virus, ~9.6 kb genome
Enveloped, lipoprotein‑rich particles
High genetic variability (7 genotypes)

sections.p: The virus uses CD81, SR‑B1 and claudin‑1 on hepatocytes for entry. Its NS5A protein interferes with JAK‑STAT pathways, limiting interferon‑stimulated gene activation.
b: Non‑cytopathic – liver injury is immune‑mediated
Rapid mutation → resistance to monotherapy

sections.p: HCV spreads mainly through blood. After entry, the RNA is translated into a polyprotein, cleaved by viral proteases, and assembled into infectious virions that are released with lipids.
b: Percutaneous exposure (IV drug use, unsafe injections)
Blood transfusion before 1992 screening
Needle‑stick injuries, tattooing with non‑sterile equipment

sections.p: Acute infection is often silent; 75‑85 % become chronic. Chronic HCV leads to progressive fibrosis, cirrhosis, and hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). Extra‑hepatic manifestations include mixed cryoglobulinemia and renal disease.
b: Acute hepatitis: mild ALT rise, jaundice in <20 %
Chronic hepatitis: persistent ALT elevation, fibrosis on imaging/biopsy
Complications: decompensated cirrhosis, HCC, portal hypertension

sections.p: Combine serology for antibodies with nucleic‑acid testing for viral RNA. Staging uses liver elastography or biopsy and the METAVIR score (F0‑F4).
b: Anti‑HCV antibody: screening, may be positive in resolved infection
HCV RNA PCR: confirms active infection, quantifies viral load
Genotype testing: guides treatment duration

t.b: Does the patient have prior exposure? Positive indicates exposure; must be followed by RNA test to confirm active infection
Is there active viral replication? Detectable RNA confirms current infection; undetectable after treatment indicates cure (SVR)
What is the degree of fibrosis? Stiffness >12 kPa suggests cirrhosis (F4); guides urgency of treatment and surveillance for HCC

sections.p: Direct‑acting antivirals (DAAs) target NS3/4A protease, NS5A, and NS5B polymerase, achieving >95 % cure rates. Treat all chronic patients regardless of stage, with priority to those with advanced fibrosis.
b: DAA regimens (e.g., NS5A inhibitor + NS5B polymerase inhibitor) – chosen for high efficacy, oral dosing, minimal side‑effects
Avoid interferon‑based therapy – poor tolerance, low SVR
Monitor ALT, bilirubin, and HCV RNA at end of treatment and 12 weeks post‑treatment

sections.p: Key points to remember for exams and clinical reasoning.
b: HCV is non‑cytopathic; liver injury is immune‑mediated
Positive anti‑HCV + detectable RNA = active infection
DAA therapy cures >95 % without interferon

whenToSeekHelp: Signs of decompensated cirrhosis: ascites, encephalopathy, variceal bleeding
Acute liver failure: INR >1.5, encephalopathy, jaundice
Sudden worsening of ALT/AST >10 × ULN with coagulopathy

faq.q: Can hepatitis C be transmitted sexually?
faq.a: Rarely; risk increases with HIV co‑infection or traumatic sexual practices.

faq.q: Why is a liver biopsy still sometimes needed?
faq.a: When non‑invasive tests are inconclusive for fibrosis stage or to assess co‑existing liver disease.

faq.q: Is there a vaccine for HCV?
faq.a: No, high genetic variability has prevented vaccine development.
